questions.q: How often does ServiceNow ship major platform releases to its customers?
options: Only when a customer specifically requests an upgrade
On a real, regular, ongoing periodic cadence — historically on the order of a couple of times a year
Only when a critical security patch is needed
Once, as a one-time migration a customer either does or skips
questions.explain: Platform releases are an ongoing, periodic fact of running on ServiceNow, not a single migration event.

questions.q: Who is responsible for planning and validating an instance's move onto a new release?
options: The customer — ServiceNow performs the technical upgrade, but planning and validation is on the customer
Nobody; it happens silently with no customer involvement at all
ServiceNow alone, with no action required from the customer at any point
A third-party auditor required by ServiceNow's contract terms
questions.explain: ServiceNow does the technical work of upgrading an instance, but staying on a supported release and validating custom work is the customer's responsibility.

questions.q: What happens if a customer falls too far behind on releases?
options: The instance stops accepting any new data until it's upgraded
The customer eventually falls off a release that has reached end of support, losing vendor support and patches
Nothing changes; every release stays supported forever
ServiceNow automatically reverses the instance to its original release
questions.explain: ServiceNow eventually ends support for older releases, which is exactly why staying reasonably current is an ongoing responsibility.

questions.q: What's the specific risk an upcoming release poses to a custom scoped application?
options: The application's data is automatically deleted during any upgrade
The application's URL changes automatically with every release
Scoped applications are immune to any effect from platform releases
Code relying on a deprecated or soon-to-be-deprecated API can fail once that release finally removes what it depended on
questions.explain: A script can run fine for years against an API that's already flagged as deprecated, right up until a release removes it.

questions.q: What is a pre-upgrade sandbox instance used for?
options: Permanently replacing the need for a production instance
Storing historical Update Sets with no other function
Validating custom applications and customizations against the new release before production is actually upgraded
Hosting the company's live production traffic during the upgrade window
questions.explain: ServiceNow upgrades this sub-production instance to the new release early, specifically so custom work can be tested before the real production upgrade happens.
